title: Virtual Triage B
subtitle: 4-year-old with a minor injury — triaging down safely
stem: Sunday evening, 6:15 pm. A father walks in holding a crying 4-year-old boy with a blood-stained towel on his head. You are the triage nurse. The waiting area already has eleven children.
parent: "He fell off the dining chair about 20 minutes ago and hit his head on the floor. There was a lot of blood. He cried straight away. He hasn't vomited. He's been talking to me the whole way here."

vitals.note: Crying loudly but stops when father speaks to him, pushes your hand away, walked in holding father's hand. 2 cm laceration over the left parietal scalp, oozing, no active bleeding. Pupils equal and reactive. No other injury.

options.text: Stable — PAT normal; minor head injury with a scalp wound
options.outcome: You settle on a reassuring first impression and move to a focused assessment.
options.note: A loud, consolable cry with normal tone and interaction is a reassuring appearance; a child who walked in and pushes you away is not critically unwell. Stable on the PAT means you have time for a focused assessment — it does not mean "nothing to do".

options.text: Unstable — neurological: raised intracranial pressure from the head injury
options.outcome: You rush him into the resuscitation bay. He stops crying when his father speaks to him and starts pulling at the monitor leads. The team asks why he is there.
options.note: Crying is not an abnormal appearance; it is the expected response of a frightened 4-year-old in pain. CNS dysfunction on the PAT means abnormal appearance with normal breathing and circulation: drowsy, floppy, not interacting, or a high-pitched inconsolable cry.

options.text: Unstable — circulation: shock from blood loss
options.outcome: You ask for IV access and fluid. He fights the cannulation; the waiting list grows while a well-perfused child takes up your time.
options.note: Scalp wounds bleed dramatically, but his circulation side is normal: pink, warm, CRT 1 s, HR 112. A towel of blood looks like more than it is. Shock from a scalp laceration alone is very rare in a 4-year-old.

options.text: Unstable — breathing affected: he is breathing fast
options.outcome: You put an oxygen mask on him. He pulls it off and cries harder. Once settled on his father's lap his breathing is quiet and regular at 24.
options.note: Crying raises the rate but there is no flaring, no recession, no abnormal sound. Work of breathing is normal. Count the rate again once he settles.

decisions.title: Intervention
decisions.prompt: He is stable on the PAT, so you have time. What is your intervention now?

options.text: Clean and dress the wound first, then ask about the fall
options.outcome: Ten minutes go into cleaning and dressing the wound. The head-injury screen still has not been done, and the next child is waiting.
options.note: Wound care can wait a few minutes; the head-injury screen cannot. If he needs a CT or a doctor urgently, you must know now.

options.text: Head-injury screen: mechanism and height of fall, loss of consciousness, vomiting (how many times), drowsiness or unusual behaviour, seizure, headache; examine the scalp for a boggy swelling and check pupils; then a full set of vital signs
options.outcome: Fall from about 60 cm, cried at once, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting, behaving normally. No boggy swelling; pupils equal and reactive. HR 108, RR 24, SpO₂ 98 %, BP 98/62.
options.note: A fall of under 1 metre with immediate cry, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting, normal behaviour, equal pupils and no boggy haematoma puts him in the low-risk group. Vital signs complete the picture.

options.text: Send him straight for a CT head; every head injury with bleeding needs imaging
options.outcome: Radiology asks for the doctor's request and the indication. You have neither; he waits in the corridor for 30 minutes.
options.note: A CT is a doctor's decision, and a low-mechanism fall with no red flags does not need one. Unnecessary CT exposes a 4-year-old to radiation. Your job is to screen and report.

options.text: Give an anti-emetic and paracetamol now so he is comfortable in the queue
options.outcome: Anti-emetic and paracetamol given. He is comfortable — and if he vomits later, the drug may hide it.
options.note: Paracetamol is reasonable, but an anti-emetic would mask vomiting, which is one of your re-triage signs. Do not treat the symptom you are relying on to detect deterioration.

decisions.key: Focused head-injury assessment first — mechanism and height of fall, loss of consciousness, vomiting, behaviour, seizure, headache; scalp and pupils — with a full set of vital signs; wound care after that.
must: head-injury screen or neurological check before wound care

decisions.title: Reassessment
decisions.label: Your reassessment
decisions.prompt: Forty minutes later the father comes to the desk: “Sister, he has vomited twice and now he wants to sleep.”

opts.v: Move him to a monitored bed and repeat the PAT and ABCDE
Let him sleep — vomiting is common after a fright
Check AVPU/GCS and the pupils
Check the blood glucose
Upgrade him to Level 2 and get the doctor now
Give an anti-emetic and put him back in the queue
Nil by mouth; head end up 30°

options.text: All the correct elements: Move him to a monitored bed and repeat the PAT and ABCDE; Check AVPU/GCS and the pupils; Upgrade him to Level 2 and get the doctor now
options.outcome: On a monitored bed: drowsy but rousable to voice, pupils equal, HR 96, BP 104/64, glucose normal. The doctor is at the bedside in four minutes.
options.note: Triage is dynamic: repeated vomiting and drowsiness after a head injury are red flags. Reassess fully, upgrade, and get the doctor now.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: You catch part of the change, but without a full set of observations nobody sees how drowsy he is getting; he is upgraded 15 minutes later. HR 88.

options.text: Let him sleep — vomiting is common after a fright
options.outcome: Twenty minutes later the father shouts from the waiting area: the boy is very hard to wake. HR 68, rouses only to pain, left pupil slightly larger than the right.

options.text: Give an anti-emetic and put him back in the queue
options.outcome: After the anti-emetic he sleeps in the queue. On your next round he rouses only to voice and his HR is 64.

decisions.title: Communication with the parents
decisions.label: Your communication with the father
decisions.prompt: The father is shaking: “Sister, is it serious? It is my fault — I left him on the chair.”

opts.v: Acknowledge his worry; do not blame him
“Children fall all the time — nothing to worry about”
Explain simply: the vomiting and sleepiness need the doctor and a scan now
Ask him to stay with his son and tell you at once if he is harder to wake, vomits again or has a fit
“Why was a four-year-old left on a chair?”
Make sure the doctor explains the CT and takes his consent

options.text: All the correct elements: Acknowledge his worry; do not blame him; Explain simply: the vomiting and sleepiness need the doctor and a scan now; Ask him to stay with his son and tell you at once if he is harder to wake, vomits again or has a fit
options.outcome: He steadies and stays at his son’s side, watching as you showed him. He understands why the scan is needed and signs the consent.
options.note: With a frightened parent: acknowledge first, explain simply and honestly, and give them a job — what to watch for and when to call.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: He nods but does not know what to watch for; he steps out to phone the family and his son is left alone on the bed.

options.text: “Children fall all the time — nothing to worry about”
options.outcome: Reassured, he takes his son out to the corridor for some air. Ten minutes later you find the boy asleep on the bench, hard to rouse.

options.text: “Why was a four-year-old left on a chair?”
options.outcome: He falls silent, guilt-stricken, and stops talking to the team; he does not tell you that his son has vomited a third time.

decisions.title: Team communication
decisions.label: Your communication with the doctor
decisions.prompt: You call the doctor. What do you say and do?

opts.v: ISBAR with the change: head injury an hour ago, vomited twice, now drowsy, rouses to voice, pupils equal, HR 96
“Doctor, please see the head-injury boy when you are free”
Ask for review now, and say why: his level of consciousness has changed
Read back the orders: CT head, neuro observations every 15 minutes
Tell the triage desk he has been upgraded so the queue is re-ordered
Send the message through the attendant

options.text: All the correct elements: ISBAR with the change: head injury an hour ago, vomited twice, now drowsy, rouses to voice, pupils equal, HR 96; Ask for review now, and say why: his level of consciousness has changed; Read back the orders: CT head, neuro observations every 15 minutes
options.outcome: “I am coming.” The doctor is at the bedside in four minutes and orders a CT head and 15-minute neuro observations; you read the orders back.
options.note: Name the change, give the numbers, ask for review now and close the loop on every order.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: The doctor has to ask what changed and how drowsy he is; the review and the CT request take longer.

options.text: “Doctor, please see the head-injury boy when you are free”
options.outcome: The doctor finishes the suturing list first. When he arrives 30 minutes later the boy rouses only to pain.

options.text: Send the message through the attendant
options.outcome: The attendant tells the doctor “the child in bed 4 is sleeping”. Nobody comes.

decisions.title: Transfer
decisions.label: Your transfer plan
decisions.prompt: The CT scanner is ready. How does he go, and where does he go after the scan?

opts.v: A nurse (and the doctor) escorts him with monitor, oxygen and suction; AVPU and pupils checked before leaving
Send him to CT with his father and the ward attendant
After the CT: admit to the HDU/PICU for neuro observations
If the CT shows a bleed: call ahead and transfer, stabilised and escorted, to a centre with paediatric neurosurgery
His CT request, notes and observation chart go with him
Send him back to the waiting area until the CT report comes

options.text: All the correct elements: A nurse (and the doctor) escorts him with monitor, oxygen and suction; AVPU and pupils checked before leaving; After the CT: admit to the HDU/PICU for neuro observations; If the CT shows a bleed: call ahead and transfer, stabilised and escorted, to a centre with paediatric neurosurgery
options.outcome: He goes to CT on the monitor with you beside him. The scan shows a small extradural haematoma; the neurosurgeon is called and he goes to theatre with his records and a clear handover.
options.note: Transport is part of care: an escort and monitoring for a drowsy child, the right destination after the scan, and a planned transfer if your hospital cannot treat what you find.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: The move happens, but not every piece was in place; the team loses time sorting out monitoring and where he should go next.

options.text: Send him to CT with his father and the ward attendant
options.outcome: In the CT room he vomits lying flat and nobody with him can suction. SpO₂ 88 %, HR 72.

options.text: Send him back to the waiting area until the CT report comes
options.outcome: Unmonitored in the waiting area he vomits again and becomes harder to rouse; the report is back before anyone looks at him.

debrief: What made him stable on the PAT, and what did your head-injury screen look for?
Which change at 40 minutes made you reassess, and why does it need the doctor now?
Which warning signs should every family be told before they wait?
takeHome: A stable PAT buys time for a focused assessment; it does not end the assessment.
Screen head injuries for red flags before wound care.
Triage down with confidence when there are no red flags — and set re-triage triggers.
Give parents specific warning signs and a route back to you.
Triage is dynamic: a change in the child changes the level, and the doctor is called now.
references: AHA PALS Provider Manual 2020: Pediatric Assessment Triangle.
NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management (2023): red flags in children.
IAP ICC PCCN Module 01: triage levels, DIRECT approach.

ending.smooth: The CT shows a small extradural haematoma. The neurosurgeon operates that night; because the change was caught early he goes home on day 4 with no deficit.
ending.detour: The CT shows an extradural haematoma. He reaches theatre, but later and drowsier than he should have, and his recovery is slower.
